tasks.description: Use a nested list comprehension to create a 3x3 multiplication table as a list of lists.
tasks.hint:
`[[i*j for j in range(1, 4)] for i in range(1, 4)]` — outer loop is rows, inner is columns.
This creates `[[1,2,3], [2,4,6], [3,6,9]]`.
Print each row with a loop: `for row in table: print(row)`
tasks.walkthrough:
The outer comprehension runs `i` from 1 to 3 and, for each, the inner one builds a row by running `j` from 1 to 3.
Each row is a list, so the result is a list of three lists. The loop prints them one per line.

tasks.description: Flatten the list `[[1, 2], [3, 4], [5, 6]]` into `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]` using a list comprehension.
tasks.hint:
`[x for sublist in nested for x in sublist]` — two `for` clauses flatten one level.
Read it left to right: for each sublist, for each x in that sublist, take x.
Alternative: `list(itertools.chain.from_iterable(nested))`
tasks.solution:
nested = [[1, 2], [3, 4], [5, 6]]
flat = [x for sublist in nested for x in sublist]
print(flat)
tasks.walkthrough:
Read the clauses in order: for each sublist in nested, then for each x in that sublist, collect x.
It's exactly the same as two nested for loops with an append inside.

tasks.description: Use a dict comprehension to invert a dictionary `{'a': 1, 'b': 2, 'c': 3}` — swap keys and values.
tasks.hint:
`{v: k for k, v in original.items()}` — swap key and value in the expression.
This only works cleanly if all values are unique (no two keys with the same value).
Result: `{1: 'a', 2: 'b', 3: 'c'}`
tasks.walkthrough:
`.items()` gives each pair, and the comprehension writes them back with value first and key second.
That only works cleanly when values are unique, which they are here.

tasks.description: Use a set comprehension to get all unique vowels in the sentence 'the quick brown fox jumps'.
tasks.hint:
`{c for c in sentence if c in 'aeiou'}` — set comprehension uses `{}` not `[]`.
Sets automatically remove duplicates — each vowel appears once.
Result will be unordered — that's fine for sets.
tasks.walkthrough:
The set comprehension collects every vowel character once, no matter how many times it appears.
`sorted` is used for printing so the output order is predictable; the set itself has no order.

tasks.description: Use a conditional expression (ternary) inside a list comprehension to label numbers 1-10 as 'even' or 'odd'.
tasks.hint:
`['even' if x % 2 == 0 else 'odd' for x in range(1, 11)]`
The ternary expression `a if condition else b` works inside comprehensions.
Result: `['odd', 'even', 'odd', 'even', ...]`
tasks.solution:
labels = ['even' if x % 2 == 0 else 'odd' for x in range(1, 11)]
print(labels)
tasks.walkthrough:
The expression at the front is a conditional: it evaluates to 'even' or 'odd' depending on the number.
Every number from 1 to 10 gets a label, so the list has ten items.

lesson.intro:
Comprehensions can do more than transform one flat list. They can nest, build
dictionaries and sets, and use conditional expressions. Used well they're
compact and clear. Used too hard they become unreadable, so today also has a
note on when to stop.

sections.heading: Nested: a list of lists
sections.body:
A comprehension inside a comprehension makes a grid. The outer one builds
rows, the inner one builds the cells of each row.

sections.heading: Flattening: two for clauses
sections.body:
Two `for` clauses in one comprehension work like nested loops, read left
to right: for each sublist, for each item in it, take the item.
sections.code:
nested = [[1, 2], [3, 4], [5, 6]]
flat = [x for sublist in nested for x in sublist]
print(flat)

sections.heading: Dict and set comprehensions
sections.body:
Curly braces with `key: value` make a dictionary. Curly braces with a
single expression make a set. Inverting a dictionary is a one-liner,
as long as the values are unique.

sections.heading: Conditional expressions inside
sections.body:
`a if condition else b` picks a value. Put it at the front of a
comprehension to label or transform items differently. Note it goes
before the `for`, unlike a filter `if`, which goes after.
sections.code:
labels = ['even' if x % 2 == 0 else 'odd' for x in range(1, 6)]
print(labels)

sections.heading: When to stop
sections.body:
If a comprehension needs more than one `if` and one `for`, or you have to
read it twice, write a loop instead. Clarity beats cleverness, and
nobody's judging line count.

watch_out: Getting the two `for` clauses backwards when flattening. The outer loop comes first.
`{}` with nothing in it is a dictionary, not a set.
A conditional expression at the front needs both `if` and `else`. A filter `if` at the end has no `else`.
Set output order isn't guaranteed. Use `sorted()` if the order matters.
